sections.title: What is an NBFC and how is one registered?

blocks.text: A **Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC)** lends and invests like a bank but is **not a bank**. It is regulated and supervised by the **RBI**. Its business includes loans and advances, buying bonds, debentures and other marketable securities (including those issued by the Government or a local authority), **leasing**, **hire-purchase**, **insurance business** and **chit business**.

blocks.title: Who is NOT an NBFC
blocks.text: An institution whose principal business is agriculture, industrial activity, buying or selling goods, providing services, or buying and selling immovable property is not an NBFC, even if it also lends.

blocks.title: Requirements for registration
rows: Must be a company registered under the Companies Act (the study material cites the 1956 Act; the 2013 Act has replaced it).
Wants to start the business of a non-banking financial institution as defined in Section 45-I(a) of the RBI Act, 1934.

blocks.title: Regulator and foreign investment
blocks.text: The RBI regulates and supervises NBFCs, not the Finance Ministry, SEBI or state governments. As per the 2024-25 exam material, up to 100% foreign investment is allowed in NBFCs for permitted activities.

NBFCs are generally **small in size and scope**, with a simple structure and **low management cost**. A few, such as provident funds and pension funds, are large. Their typical features are listed below.

blocks.title: Key features
rows: Very little owned capital. They collect larger sums from the public by offering attractive returns because they find it hard to gather deposits.
Borrowers turned down by commercial banks and development banks come to NBFCs, which lend easily with few documents.
Loans are given with little or inadequate security, so they are riskier and harder to recover.
Unrecovered short and medium-term loans are converted into long-term loans, which raises the amount, term and rate of interest.
Credit for agriculture, industry, trade and services, and household finance for consumption, education, home construction, vehicles and health.

blocks.title: Five features: L-E-U-R-S
blocks.phrase: Lenders Easily Use Risky Schemes: Low capital, Easy loans, Unsecured, Rescheduling, Support for needs.

blocks.title: What an NBFC cannot do
rows: Part of it; issues cheques drawn on itself
Not part of it; cannot issue cheques drawn on itself
Insured up to the DICGC limit
RBI does not guarantee repayment of NBFC deposits

blocks.title: Ombudsman note
blocks.text: Older study notes say there is no Ombudsman for NBFC complaints, apart from credit card complaints against a bank-owned NBFC, which can go to the Banking Ombudsman if the NBFC does not reply satisfactorily within 30 days. The RBI later introduced an Ombudsman Scheme for NBFCs (2018), where the appellate authority is the RBI Deputy Governor in charge.

blocks.title: Three things an NBFC lacks: D-C-I
blocks.phrase: NBFCs have no DCI: Demand deposits, Cheques on itself, Insurance of deposits (DICGC).
letters: Cannot issue cheques drawn on itself or join the payment system

blocks.title: Ten categories and the numbers that define them
rows: Finances physical assets that support productive or economic activity
Financing of such assets and income from it at least 60% of total assets and total income
Provides finance by loans or advances for activities other than its own; does not include an AFC
At least 75% of assets in infrastructure loans; NOF ₹300 crore; credit rating A or equivalent; CRAR 15%
Holds shares and securities of group companies, takes public funds
Asset size ₹100 crore or more; at least 90% of assets in group-company investments; at least 60% in equity shares of group companies
Channels long-term debt into infrastructure projects through rupee or dollar bonds
Bonds of minimum 5-year maturity; sponsored through Infrastructure Finance Companies
At least 85% of assets are qualifying assets; loan up to ₹50,000 in the first cycle and ₹1,00,000 in later cycles
Non-deposit NBFC whose principal business is factoring
Factoring assets at least 50% of total assets
At least 90% of turnover or gross income from mortgage guarantee business; NOF ₹100 crore
Financial institution through which promoters can set up a new bank

blocks.text: A **Core Investment Company** does not trade in its group-company shares, debt or loans except through block sales for dilution or disinvestment, and it does not carry on other financial activities beyond permitted ones such as holding bank deposits, money market instruments, government securities, and loans to or guarantees for group companies.

blocks.title: Ten NBFC types in order
blocks.phrase: All Industrious Learners Improve Concepts, Investigating Many Factors, Making Notes.

blocks.title: Percentages that matter
blocks.phrase: Sixty asset, seventy-five infra, eighty-five micro, ninety core and mortgage, fifty factors.
letters: Asset Finance Company: assets and income from financing physical assets
Infrastructure Finance Company: assets in infrastructure loans
Core Investment Company (group assets) and Mortgage Guarantee (turnover or income)
NBFC-Factors: factoring assets in total assets
blocks.note: A CIC also needs at least 60% of assets in group-company equity.

blocks.title: Important regulations
items: NBFCs may accept or renew public deposits for a minimum of **12 months** and a maximum of **60 months**.
They cannot accept deposits repayable on demand.
The interest rate is prescribed by the RBI from time to time; the ceiling then was **12.5% per annum**, paid or compounded at rests not shorter than monthly.
NBFCs cannot offer gifts, incentives or any other additional benefit to depositors.
They must have a minimum investment grade credit rating.
Deposits with NBFCs are **not insured**, and repayment is **not guaranteed by the RBI**.

blocks.title: Deposit window: 12 to 60
blocks.phrase: A year to five years, no demand, no gifts, rate capped at twelve and a half.
letters: Ceiling on interest rate per annum (study material)
Zero insurance and zero RBI guarantee

sections.title: Chit funds, CIS, Ponzi schemes and CIBIL

blocks.title: Who regulates what
rows: Governed by the **Chit Funds Act, 1982**, a Central Act administered by state governments.

blocks.text: **Money circulation, multi-level or chain marketing and Ponzi schemes** promise easy or quick money for enrolling members. Their income does not come mainly from selling products but from **enrolling more and more members** and charging heavy subscription fees. They collapse when new recruits dry up.

blocks.title: Peer-to-peer (P2P) and credit score facts
rows: RBI capped a single lender's total exposure across all P2P platforms and a single borrower's total loans across all platforms at ₹10 lakh each (limits may have been revised since).
Used by banks and NBFCs to judge creditworthiness; it is a **3-digit number**.

blocks.title: Takeover norm
blocks.text: The RBI said that buying a stake of 26% or more in an NBFC, or a change of more than 30% of its directors, needs prior RBI permission.

revision: NBFCs lend, invest, lease, do hire-purchase, insurance and chit business; they are regulated by the RBI and are not banks.
Minimum NOF for NBFC registration: ₹200 lakh; company must fall under Section 45-I(a) of the RBI Act, 1934.
NBFC features: low capital, easy loans, unsecured lending, rescheduling of loans, support for economic needs.
NBFCs cannot accept demand deposits, issue cheques on themselves or give DICGC deposit insurance.
NBFC deposits: minimum 12 months, maximum 60 months; ceiling 12.5% p.a.; no gifts; not insured; no RBI guarantee.
Asset Finance Company: at least 60% of assets and income from financing physical assets.
Infrastructure Finance Company: 75% infra assets, NOF ₹300 crore, rating A, CRAR 15%.
Systemically Important CIC: assets of ₹100 crore or more, 90% in group companies, 60% in group equity.
NBFC-MFI: 85% qualifying assets; loans up to ₹50,000 first cycle and ₹1,00,000 later cycles.
NBFC-Factors: factoring assets at least 50% of total assets.
Mortgage Guarantee Company: 90% of turnover or income from guarantees; NOF ₹100 crore.
Infrastructure Debt Fund: bonds of minimum 5-year maturity, sponsored through IFCs; NOFHC is the route to set up a bank.
SEBI regulates CIS; chit funds come under the Chit Funds Act, 1982 administered by states.
Ponzi and multi-level schemes earn from enrolling members, not from selling products.
CIBIL score is a 3-digit number used by banks and NBFCs; P2P limit under the 2017 directions was ₹10 lakh each.
